title: Design compute: workload requirements, VMs and containers
learningObjective: Specify compute components from workload requirements, and recommend VM-based and container-based solutions.
foundation: Choose compute by asking how much control you need. The less you manage, the more time you spend on the app.
From least to most control: serverless functions, App Service, Container Apps, Kubernetes (AKS), virtual machines.
Then size it, decide how it scales, and pick the cheapest pricing that still fits.
engineer: Requirements to components: hosting model (code or container), OS and runtime needs, scale pattern (steady, bursty, event-driven, scale to zero), state, network isolation (VNet integration, private endpoints), availability (zones, regions), compliance (dedicated hosts, confidential computing), and cost model. The Azure compute decision tree in the Architecture Center starts from lift-and-shift versus cloud-optimised.

VM-based: size families (B burstable, D general purpose, E memory, F compute, L storage, M large memory, N GPU, H HPC), Trusted Launch and confidential VMs, managed disk types, Virtual Machine Scale Sets (Flexible) for scale-out, availability zones, proximity placement groups for latency, Azure Dedicated Host for single-tenant physical servers, Spot VMs for interruptible work, reservations or savings plans and Azure Hybrid Benefit for steady workloads, Azure Virtual Desktop for desktops and apps, and Azure VMware Solution to run VMware workloads natively.

Container-based: Azure Container Apps (serverless microservices, KEDA scaling to zero, revisions, Dapr, jobs), AKS (full Kubernetes API, node pools, operators, service mesh; AKS Automatic simplifies operations), Azure Container Instances (single container groups on demand), App Service for containers (web apps in containers), Azure Container Registry (Premium for geo-replication and private endpoints).

animation.caption: Pick the compute service, then the VM pricing and placement option.

example.title: Choosing compute for a logistics platform
body: The customer portal runs on App Service; ten microservices run on Container Apps scaling on queue length; the routing engine with custom operators runs on AKS.
A legacy Windows app moves as-is to VMs in a zone-spread scale set with reservations; nightly re-optimisation jobs use Spot VMs; dispatchers get Azure Virtual Desktop.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription; most design reviews need only Reader access
permissions: Reader to review existing resources; Contributor or Owner to build the design
limits: Check service limits and regional availability for each component
portal: Create a resource: App Service / Container Apps / Kubernetes service / Virtual machine.
VM > Size, Availability options (zones, scale set), Spot discount.
configuration.cli:
az containerapp create -g rg-app -n orders --environment cae-prod --image acrcontoso.azurecr.io/orders:1.0 --min-replicas 0 --max-replicas 30
az vm create -g rg-batch -n vm-spot01 --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_D4s_v5 --priority Spot --eviction-policy Deallocate --max-price -1

troubleshooting.cause: Azure evicted the Spot VMs for capacity.
troubleshooting.fix: Use Spot only for interruptible work and checkpoint progress.

troubleshooting.symptom: Small team overwhelmed by AKS upgrades and node management.
troubleshooting.fix: Consider Container Apps or AKS Automatic.

comparisons.difference: Container Apps: serverless, no cluster to manage; AKS: full Kubernetes control.
Reservations: committed steady use at a discount; Spot: spare capacity, evictable, deepest discount.

misconceptions.reality: Container Apps and ACI run containers without managing a cluster.

misconceptions.myth: VMs are the default for migration.
misconceptions.reality: They are the fastest path, but PaaS reduces long-term operations.

architectureDecisions: Start at the most managed compute and move down only for a reason.
Right-size VMs and use reservations/Hybrid Benefit for steady use.
Container Apps for microservices; AKS when you need Kubernetes itself.

walkthrough.subtitle: Run each workload on the most managed compute that meets its needs, at the right size and price.

steps.label: Problem
steps.title: Many workloads, many compute options
body: Web apps, microservices, a legacy Windows app and nightly batch jobs all need somewhere to run.

steps.label: Ladder
steps.title: Less to manage at the top
body: Functions and App Service: you bring code. Container Apps: you bring containers, Azure runs them. AKS: you run Kubernetes. VMs: you run everything.

callout.text: Move down the ladder only when a requirement forces you to.

steps.label: VMs
steps.title: Size, scale, pay less
body: Pick the size family by CPU, memory, GPU or storage needs. Scale sets add VMs with load. Spot VMs for work that can be interrupted; reservations or savings plans for VMs that run all the time.

steps.label: Containers
steps.title: Container Apps or AKS
body: Container Apps runs microservices without a cluster and scales to zero. AKS gives full Kubernetes when you need operators, custom networking or node control.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Compute design
body: Least management that meets the need.
recap: Functions → App Service → Container Apps → AKS → VMs
VM family, scale sets, Spot, reservations
Container Apps for microservices; AKS for Kubernetes control

handsOn.title: Compare compute options with the pricing calculator
handsOn.cost: Free. Uses the public Azure pricing calculator; nothing is deployed.
before: A browser. No Azure sign-in is needed.

steps.do: Open azure.microsoft.com/pricing/calculator. Add a Virtual Machines estimate: your region, D2s v5, Linux, 730 hours.
In the same item, switch savings options to 1-year and 3-year reserved, then Spot (if shown).
steps.see: Large discounts for commitment; the deepest for Spot.

steps.do: Add an App Service estimate: Linux, Premium v3 P1v3, 1 instance.
steps.see: A price for managed web hosting (no OS to patch).

steps.do: Add an Azure Container Apps estimate (Consumption) with a few million requests and a modest vCPU-second usage.
steps.see: Usage-based cost that can drop near zero when idle.

steps.do: Compare the three for a small web API that is idle at night.
steps.see: Container Apps or App Service usually cost less to operate than a VM you must patch.

check: You can explain when reservations, Spot and serverless each save money.
